Ratoon sprouting poorly after a December-January harvest: what to do
Stubble buds sprout slowly in the cold. Do this 45-day count before you plough the field.
Intercrop
December-January harvest: ratoon sprouting poorly? | ganna.in
Why cane cut in the cold sprouts slowly as ratoon, what to do in the first 45 days, when to fill gaps and how much variety matters.
Poor ratoon sprouting in the cold
How many days does a winter-cut ratoon take to sprout?
No fixed day can be given. It varies with the cold, the variety and soil moisture. Counting on day 45 and deciding then is a sensible approach.
If the field looks empty at first, should I plough it?
No, not right away. Stubble buds sprout late in the cold. Count on day 45, then fill gaps or take advice from your agriculture officer.
Is the effect this large in Gujarat too?
The studies we read are from North India. South Gujarat has a milder winter, so the effect may be smaller, but we did not find exact figures for it.
December-January harvest: ratoon sprouting poorly?

9 November 2026 · Gafar Laiya, Gujarat Bio Organics Pvt. Ltd.

Stubble buds of cane harvested in the cold sprout slowly and in smaller numbers. So do not panic and plough the field straight away. Cut the stubble level with the ground, keep the soil moist, count on day 45, and then fill the empty patches. Decide whether to keep the ratoon only after that.
Why does the ratoon slow down in the cold?

A ratoon crop grows from the buds on the stubble below the soil. According to a 2018 Indian Farming article, these buds sprout late at low temperatures. Even in normal conditions only 30 to 40% of stubble buds sprout. So if the field looks empty early on, do not write it off yet.

Studies also show an effect of the harvest month. In a 2003 Sugar Tech study on CoLk 8102 and CoS 88230, sprouting was lower in crops cut in December and January than in those cut in November and February. A Journal of Sugarcane Research report from Karnal also found average sprouting higher in spring-cut crops than in winter-cut crops.

Keep in mindThese trials are from North India, where winter temperatures can fall to 0 to 5°C. South Gujarat has a milder winter, so the effect there may be smaller. We did not find exact figures for South Gujarat. For local information, ask Navsari Agricultural University or your agriculture officer.
What to do in the first 45 days after harvest
Stubble: Cut level with the ground using a sharp knife. Take care not to shake or uproot the clump, or the plant count will fall.
Irrigation: Irrigate on time after harvest. A 2021 Indian Farming article says a ratoon crop needs 8 to 10 irrigations over its life. Where water is short, drip is useful.

Trash: Do not burn it. The same article mentions spreading 3 tonnes of trash per hectare between the furrows, which is about 480 to 490 kg per vigha. For details read Burn the trash or keep it in the field?

Count on day 45: In the Karnal trial, sprouting was recorded 45 days after harvest. Count on the same day in 4 to 5 different parts of your field. Note where sprouting is good and where there are empty strips.
How much does variety matter?

Not every variety sprouts equally in the cold. In the Sugar Tech study, CoLk 8102 had more sprouts per clump. Work at Karnal on more than 7,000 clones found large differences in winter sprouting, and some clones sprouted even better in winter. So when you plant next, ask: how does this variety ratoon after a winter harvest?
Fill the gaps, or not keep the ratoon at all?
If empty strips remain after 45 days, consider gap filling. Polybag settlings 35 to 40 days old, or clumps from dense patches, can be used. For the method read How to fill gaps in a ratoon crop.

No single figure for how much gap means dropping the ratoon applies to every field. But if the field has red rot or another serious disease, do not keep the ratoon. If in doubt, show photos to your agriculture officer.
If you can control the harvest date

According to the 2021 Indian Farming article, spring-harvested crops make better ratoons because of moderate temperatures. The harvest date usually depends on the mill schedule, so this is not always possible. But if you have more than one field, you can try to keep the field you plan to ratoon from being cut in mid-winter. It is easier to let the crop you will not ratoon be the one harvested in December-January.

About chemicalsSome research has used growth regulators to improve ratoon sprouting, but that was in trials. Do not decide a dose or timing on your own. Ask your local agriculture officer for pesticide and chemical choice.

Identifying smut
How do I count 10% infection?
Count 100 clumps in different parts of the field. If more than 10 of them have whips, TNAU advises not keeping the ratoon.
Is it enough to just cut off the whip?
Cutting alone does not remove the infection in the clump, and the powder can fly while cutting. Bag the whip first, then uproot and destroy the clump.
Black whip on sugarcane: what to do about smut
Home › Blog › Identifying smut

A long black whip at the top of the cane may be whip smut. Bag the whip before it bursts, uproot and destroy the clump, and do not take setts from this field. If more than 10% of clumps are infected, do not keep the ratoon.
How to identify smut
Look for these symptoms, as listed by Tamil Nadu Agricultural University (TNAU):
Whip: A whip-like structure 25 to 150 cm long grows from the top of the cane.
Covering: At first the whip is covered by a thin silvery membrane, with black powder inside.
Cane: Infected cane turns thin, with long internodes early on and shorter ones later.
Clump: Especially in ratoon, side buds sprout heavily and leaves stay narrow and upright.
Confirm itDo not decide from a photo alone. Show the clump count and photos to your agriculture officer or agriculture university.
Why one clump can put the whole field at risk

According to the South African research body SASRI, an infected clump releases billions of spores. Wind can carry them to nearby fields, and rain and irrigation water spread them too. Spores infect sprouting buds and new shoots, so the period after planting and after harvest matters. Infected setts also take the disease to new fields. In dry soil spores can survive for at least 6 months.
What to do if you see a whip in the field
Bag the whip: Do not shake it. Slip a gunny or plastic bag over it and close it gently. TNAU then advises keeping the bag in boiling water for 1 hour.
Remove the clump: Uproot the whole diseased clump and destroy it by burning. Take care that whip powder does not fall on other clumps.
Check again and again: SASRI advises checking the field every 4 to 8 weeks. New infected clumps can appear after a clean-up.
Count: Count 100 clumps in different parts of the field and note how many are diseased. Your ratoon decision comes from this number.
Keep the ratoon or not?

TNAU advises against keeping the ratoon when infection is above 10%. That means if more than 10 of 100 clumps have whips, the field is not fit for ratoon. Even at lower infection, keep checking regularly. If the ratoon sprouts poorly, also read Poor ratoon sprouting in the cold.

When you clear the field, remove the old stubble thoroughly. SASRI says clumps left behind can regrow and become a source of infection later. It advises keeping the field empty for at least 3 months after the last regrowth is removed. If possible, irrigate the field two weeks before replanting so spores in the soil germinate and die.
What to watch for when taking setts
Seed: Do not take setts from a smut-affected field at all. Take them only from a checked, healthy field.

Hot water: TNAU gives hot water treatment at 50°C for 30 minutes or 52°C for 18 minutes. Keeping the temperature exact needs a thermometer and a proper tank. Ask your Krishi Vigyan Kendra where this facility is available.
Variety: A resistant variety helps, but SASRI says it can still be infected under heavy disease pressure. Ask your agriculture university which variety suits your area now.
Pigeon pea: According to TNAU, growing pigeon pea between the rows can reduce further spread.
Red rot is a different disease from smut. To identify it, read How to identify red rot. For pesticide choice, ask your local agriculture officer.

Single-bud setts direct in the field or nursery settlings: know this difference before you save seed
Want to save seed? Direct single-bud setts and nursery settlings are not the same thing. See what a trial found.
Single-bud setts direct or nursery settlings? | ganna.in
What is the difference between planting single-bud setts direct and transplanting nursery settlings? Trial figures, seed saving and how to choose.
Single-bud setts or settlings
Can single-bud setts be planted direct?
They can, but in a Punjab trial germination and yield were lower than with 2 to 3-bud setts. If you want to save seed, look at the nursery settling method.
At what age should nursery settlings be transplanted?
According to the Indian Farming article, single-bud settlings are transplanted at 25 to 35 days and bud-chip settlings at 6 to 8 weeks.
Does saving seed raise yield?
There is no such guarantee. The saving is in seed. Yield depends on soil, water, variety and management.
Single-bud setts direct or nursery settlings?
Home › Blog › Single-bud setts or settlings

Do not plant single-bud setts directly in the field just to save seed. In a Punjab trial, germination and yield were lower than with 2 to 3-bud setts. To save seed, look at raising single-bud settlings in a nursery and transplanting them, and count the extra nursery and transplanting work.
Where is the difference?
Many farmers hear "single bud" and treat two different methods as one.
Single-bud setts direct in the field: A small piece goes straight into the furrow. Germination depends on field moisture and conditions.

Nursery settlings: A seedling is raised in a nursery from a single bud or bud chip, then transplanted. A 2025 Indian Farming article by ICAR-IARI authors says single-bud settlings are transplanted at 25 to 35 days and bud-chip settlings at 6 to 8 weeks.
What the Punjab trial found
A three-year trial on spring planting was run at the Punjab Agricultural University station in Faridkot. The results appeared in the Journal of Sugarcane Research in 2013.
3-bud setts: germination 31.6%, yield 64.7 t per hectare.
2-bud setts: germination 32.2%, yield 64.9 t per hectare.
1-bud setts direct: germination 25.1%, yield 48.1 t per hectare.

These are trial figuresThey are three-year averages from one location, not a promise. In your field results vary with soil, water, weather, variety and management. Punjab and South Gujarat have different weather.

In this trial there was no real yield difference between 2 and 3 buds. So if 3-bud setts are not available, 2-bud setts are an option. But planting a single bud direct cut yield sharply in this trial.
How much seed does the nursery method save?
The figures in the 2025 Indian Farming article are:
Normal 2 to 3-bud setts: 6 to 8 t per hectare, or about 1 to 1.3 t per vigha.
Single-bud settlings (spaced transplanting): the article gives about 1 to 2 t per hectare, or roughly 160 to 320 kg per vigha.
Bud chip: 8 to 10 quintals per hectare, or about 130 to 160 kg per vigha.

The same article gives transplant spacing of 90 x 90 cm or 120 x 60 cm. It says seed is about 20% of total cultivation cost, so the saving is a real point. But with it come nursery space, water, daily care and transplanting labour. Work out both sides before you decide.
Which method should you choose?
If good seed is not short: Healthy 2 to 3-bud setts are the simple route. For details read Sugarcane planting.
If seed of a new variety is short: Nursery settlings are useful where you must cover more field with little seed.
For gap filling: Keeping a few polybag settlings ready makes the job easier. See How to fill gaps.
If you cannot look after a nursery: If you cannot give daily water and attention, stay with direct 2 to 3-bud setts.
With any method, healthy seed comes first. Do not take buds or setts from a field with red rot or smut. If you get germination gaps, also read Why germination gaps happen.
